title: Two answers out of one call

prereqs.why: Two references carry results out, and a const reference carries the input in without copying it.
The whole container is passed to the function, which is where the cost of copying starts to matter.

statement:
Write a function

```cpp
void extremes(const std::vector<int>& values, int& lowest, int& highest);
```

that finds the smallest and largest of `values` and writes them
into `lowest` and `highest`. Read integers until the input runs
out and report:

```
input:   4 -3 9 0 7

output:  min -3
         max 9
```

If there were no numbers, print `empty` on its own and do not call
the function — there is nothing for it to report.

### The point of the problem

A function can only `return` one thing. When two results belong
together, the usual answer in C++ is reference parameters:

```cpp
int lo{};
int hi{};
extremes(values, lo, hi);        // both filled in by the call
```

Notice the three parameter types, and that all three are
deliberate:

```
const std::vector<int>&     in     — do not copy, do not modify
int&                        out    — write the answer here
int&                        out
```

**Why `const` and `&` on the input.** Passing a vector by value
copies every element. For ten thousand `int`s that is 40 KB copied
for no reason. The `&` prevents the copy; the `const` then promises
the function will not modify it, which both documents the intention
and lets the compiler stop you breaking it.

**Why not `const` on the outputs.** They exist to be written to.
A reader of the declaration can tell input from output by the
`const` alone, which is most of why the convention is worth
following.

### Constraints

Each number is between -1,000,000 and 1,000,000, and there are at
most 10,000 of them, possibly none.

### Boundary cases

- **No numbers.** The function is not called at all. It has no
  sensible values to write, and writing nothing while the caller
  prints whatever `lo` happened to hold would be worse.
- **One number** is both the minimum and the maximum.
- **All negative.** `-4 -9 -1` has a maximum of -1, which is what
  catches starting the maximum at 0.
- **All equal** gives the same number twice.

### What the grader checks

Submitting runs your program on the cases above and on hidden
ones, and then compiles it a second time with a `main` of this
exercise’s own that calls `extremes` directly and reads
`lowest` and `highest` back afterwards. Before each call they hold
values that are not the answer, so a function that prints the two lines
itself and never writes through its references — which produces
identical output — fails here.
hints: Read everything into a `std::vector<int>` first, then decide whether to call the function at all. The empty case is the caller’s problem, not the function’s.
Inside the function, start both answers at `values[0]` and walk from index 1. That avoids inventing a starting value, and it is safe because the caller guarantees the vector is not empty.
The input parameter is `const std::vector<int>&`. Leaving the `&` off copies the whole vector on every call; leaving the `const` off compiles but stops saying that the function does not modify it.
